h1: Styrian Aurora hops for floral bitterness in lagers
title: Styrian Aurora Hops for Floral Lager | Craft Beer School
desc: Styrian Aurora is a Slovenian hop with smooth bitterness and a floral, citrus aroma. Where it works in a lager and how to dose it.
teaser: Styrian Aurora bitters smoothly and smells of flowers and citrus. It is a quiet upgrade for a pale lager.
standfirst: Styrian Aurora is a Slovenian hop that gives clean, rounded bitterness and a soft floral, citrus aroma. For a lager brewer who wants more than a neutral bittering hop, it is a useful middle path.
sections: A Slovenian hop with a long career

Aurora is grown in the Savinja valley of Slovenia, in the historic region of Styria, which is why brewers often call it Styrian Aurora. It was bred at the hop institute in Žalec. Alpha acids typically fall around 7 to 9%, which sits between a noble aroma hop and a modern high alpha bittering hop.

That middle position is why it is useful. It has enough alpha acid to carry a lager's bitterness with a moderate weight of hops. It also has enough aroma to be worth adding late.
What it adds to a lager

Tasters report floral and citrus aroma, light honey and a gentle spice. Bitterness is described as smooth, which fits the hop's modest cohumulone content. Harsh bitterness in a lager shows up as a lingering sharpness on the back of the tongue. A smoother hop reduces it.

Aurora is not a dramatic hop. It fits pale lagers, Helles, Pilsner and golden ales where the brewer wants floral lift without the grassy sharpness some noble hops bring. See our guide to bittering hops for clean lager bitterness for the wider choice.
A worked hop bill for 1,000 litres

For a pale lager at 20 IBU, use Aurora at 8% alpha with 25% utilisation in a 60 minute boil. The charge is 20 x 1,000 / (0.08 x 0.25 x 1,000) = 1,000 g, or 1 g per litre.

For more character, split the hop bill:

  • 60 minutes: 600 g for about 12 IBU.
  • 10 minutes: 400 g for about 3 IBU and a first layer of flavour.
  • Whirlpool at 80 °C for 15 minutes: 500 g, mainly for aroma.

The late additions add a few more IBU, so brew once, measure and trim the 60 minute charge next time. Utilisation moves with kettle shape, boil vigour and wort gravity.

Floral aromas depend on the dose. Too much late hop in a delicate lager reads as soap or potpourri. Keep the whirlpool charge under 1 g per litre for a pale lager. Taste the cooled wort first: if it smells like a bunch of flowers, the finished beer will probably still be too floral, even after fermentation has scrubbed off some of the volatiles.

The malt matters too. Pilsner malt keeps the hop in focus. If you tint an amber lager with a malt extract such as SINAMAR, the floral note stays readable because colour comes without roasty astringency. Heavy roast would bury it.

Ferment at 9 to 12 °C. Raise the tank to 14 to 15 °C for two days when fermentation is nearly done to let the yeast reabsorb diacetyl. Then cool and lager for at least three weeks. Floral hop notes need time to settle into the malt. Yeast needs time to clean up after itself.

If you must shorten the schedule for cash flow reasons, use a lower hop rate. Fresh, rushed lagers show rough edges. An aromatic hop highlights them instead of hiding them.
Water and mash for a soft finish

A floral hop needs a gentle background. Soft water with calcium under 50 mg/L and low sulphate keeps bitterness rounded, much as in classic Pilsner brewing. Hard borewell water pushes the other way: high sulphate sharpens bitterness and makes a smooth hop taste rough.

If your supply is hard, cut it with reverse osmosis water until the mix is soft. Then add a small amount of calcium chloride for yeast health. Mash at 5.3 to 5.4 pH and keep the sparge liquor acidified. A well-built water profile does more for lager bitterness than any hop swap.
Buying and storing it in India

Aurora is easier to find than rarer European hops and is often sold in vacuum packed pellets. Ask the importer for the harvest year and for a certificate of analysis showing alpha acid. Alpha falls as hops age, so a lot that tested 8% last year may now sit nearer 7%. Recalculate your bitterness charge each time you open a new pack.

Store frozen in the original foil. Once a pack is open, use it within weeks, not months.

Take your usual pale lager and replace the bittering hop with Aurora at the same IBU. Add 0.3 g per litre at whirlpool. Taste it next to the original at eight weeks. Notice the finish, whether the beer lingers or stops. Note whether the aroma changes the way a drinker would describe the beer. You have learned something about hop selection that you can apply to every recipe.
faqs: What does Styrian Aurora taste like?
Floral and citrus, with light honey and spice. It is gentle with smooth bitterness.
Is Aurora a bittering or aroma hop?
Both. Alpha acids around 7 to 9% suit bittering. The aroma is pleasant enough for late additions.
Can I use Aurora in an IPA?
Yes, though its character is subtle. It works best as a supporting hop alongside stronger American or New Zealand varieties.
